newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Small plane, big hop for Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Small plane, big hop for Hong Kong.

text.p: It wasn't a jumbo jet or Concorde, just a light plane carrying a handful of passengers.
But the first plane to touch down on the brand new runway at Hong Kong's ambitious new Chek Lap Kok airport on Thursday marks a special triumph for the British colony.
Chek Lap Kok is not due to open until April 1998, replacing congested Kai Tak airport, and Thursday's flight carrying Hong Kong officials was a symbolic one.

"It passes quite a significant milestone for us. In the past five years we've taken what was sea and a small island and created an airport about the size of Heathrow," said airport spokesman Philip Bruce.
But it also signals the final burying of the fears, suspicions and downright hostility that marked the middle years of Hong Kong's drawn-out transition to Chinese rule.
Nothing symbolised the chill between Britain and China over Hong Kong more than the US$20.3 billion airport, part of what was then the world's most expensive infrastructure project.
It was born in the dark days that followed the Tiananmen massacre of June 1989, which savagely ruptured Hong Kong's confidence in its future as a part of China.

Gloom descended on the territory. A rush for foreign passports snowballed. The promises made in the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration governing the handover of Hong Kong to China in mid-1997 suddenly looked hollow.

So when then Governor David Wilson stood up to declare Hong Kong would embark on an ambitious airport and port project he sold it to Hong Kong's depressed population as a glittering symbol of British confidence in Hong Kong's future and in its continued role as a leading Asian trading entrepot.

He reminded Hong Kong that China had promised Hong Kong considerable autonomy in running its affairs. That capitalism would continue in Hong Kong and the wealthy community of six million people would continue to enjoy their freedoms and fiscal independence for 50 years.
These reassurances fell flat when China then stepped in. It coldly informed the outgoing British colonial government that Beijing held the trump card.
Unless it gave its blessing, there would be no endorsement and therefore no financing. The bankers wanted guarantees before Hong Kong could tap the capital markets to fund the airport.

The airport was a hostage to Sino-British wrangling. For five years China argued the project was unnecesarily expensive and accused the British of squandering Hong Kong's vast reserves, of constructing a huge white elephant in order to give British firms contracts, charges Britain denied.

The impasse reached the stage where newly-elected Prime Minister John Major visited Beijing in 1991 to break the log-jam, becoming the first western leader to visit since the tanks rolled into Tiananmen, crushing the pro-democracy protest movement.
Agreement was slow in coming. A clause here, a breakthrough there. It took until June 1995 before the decks were cleared and China and Britain finally put the disagreement behind them.
Yet throughout the political wrangling and the inevitable toll of confidence in Hong Kong, somehow work progressed.
An army of people representing just about every nation under the sun laboured away, decapitating a mountain, levelling a small island, reclaiming the ocean. An airport emerged from the sea.
The airport authority's Bruce doubts the new airport will ever reach full capacity. "We expect when we open, the airport will have a capacity of 35 million passengers a year."
It could accommodate up to 87 million people when a second runway is completed, he said.
"By the time you get to 87 million passengers a year... by the time you get up to that level, you'll be beaming up to the Starship Enterprise. "You won't be using aeroplanes by then."
